newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Eurotunnel concession deal hope by EGM.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurotunnel concession deal hope by EGM.

text.p: Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel said on Tuesday it hoped to reach by its July 10 extraordinary meeting an agreement in principle with France and Britain to extend its concession to run the tunnel.

Eurotunnel has been in talks since last autumn to extend its 65-year-operating concession but was hampered by delays due to elections in both countries, leaving the group in a race against time to secure the extension ahead of a vital shareholder meeting to approve its restructuring rescue plan.
As expected, Eurotunnel, which is strapped by a debt of about nine billion pounds ($15 billion), confirmed the meeting had been pushed back after Tuesday's meeting failed to attract a quorum.
It hopes an extended concession will enhance its chances of getting shareholder clearance for its debt deal.

Eurotunnel urged all shareholders to approve the debt restructuring at the meeting as French investors whipped up opposition to the terms of the restructuring deal, claiming on Monday they had enough votes for a blocking minority on July 10.
But joint chairman Patrick Ponsolle warned that the debt-crippled company could risk insolvency if shareholders failed to back the restructuring.
"It is now or never," he said in a statement.

"A failure to approve the plan risks the loss of everything ... There is nothing to be gained, and everything to lose, by turning down the restructuring plan which has been submitted for approval," he added.
His comments followed earlier warnings given in an interview with the French newspaper Les Echos on Tuesday.
"If there is a 'no' vote at the shareholders' meeting, it will be extremely difficult to avoid bankruptcy," he said in the interview.
"It is an illusion to imagine that the banks would be ready to negotiate a new plan if a minority of shareholders blocked agreement to the current one," Ponsolle said.
Many of the banks, located in several countries, already found the terms of the restructuring too generous, he said.

As the stakes rise between creditor banks and shareholders ahead of that meeting, the radical ADACTE group and more moderate Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association both said they could have enough votes to control the outcome.
Another shareholder force is led by French lawyer Sophie L'Helias, who represents small and institutional investors.

She has set tough conditions on backing the plan, including that creditor banks abandon 25 percent of their loans and the possibility of a "right of substitution" which would ultimately allow the banks to take over Eurotunnel's cash-flow.
Ponsolle said the banks would exercise this right if the shareholders blocked the plan and this would give them control of its cash-flow for several decades.
He said the "double or quits" strategy of big fund managers, whose Eurotunnel investments were a tiny part of their empires, had little in common with the interests of ordinary investors.
The market was unmoved on the statement. Eurotunnel's shares were down one pence at 66 1/2 by 1145 GMT in London.
The group's earlier statement also reported that latest operational figures indicated its first half results would be ahead of budget.
Ponsolle added that the level of traffic for its heavy goods vehicles shuttle service was exceeding 1,000 lorries per day.
($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
